Chapter One: Grocery Store Aisles and the Weight of Memory
You know, there’s a certain ache that creeps in when you least expect it. Maybe for you, it’s a song that drifts through the car speakers, or a street corner that brings back a wave of nostalgia. But for some, it’s the bright, humming aisles of a grocery store—where the scent of ripe fruit and the neat rows of packages suddenly open a portal to another life.
Imagine this: Standing in the heart of a bustling Asian supermarket, a young woman is surrounded by shelves lined with dried seaweed, jars of fermented vegetables, and the gentle chatter of shoppers speaking a language she only half understands. Every item she passes seems to carry the weight of memory, each one a quiet reminder of a mother who’s no longer there.
Isn’t it easy to forget how food can become its own language? Especially when you’re growing up between two cultures. For kids of immigrants, the kitchen isn’t just a place to eat—it’s the very first classroom. The dinner table? That’s where love gets measured, not in words, but in spoonfuls and side dishes. A mother’s hands are always moving—chopping, stirring, tasting, and quietly showing the way. The lessons are never formal: rinse the rice until the water runs clear, trust your nose to pick the sweetest melon, fold the dumplings just so, so they won’t burst in the pot. These everyday rituals turn into a kind of inheritance, passed down with every repetition and gentle correction.
But here’s something to pay attention to. When loss arrives, it doesn’t just take the person you loved. It pulls loose all the threads that held your sense of self together. Suddenly, the grocery store—a place you’ve visited a hundred times—becomes a test. Which brand of soy sauce did she always reach for? How did she get the broth to taste just right? The answers feel lost in the past, and every time you try to recreate a favorite dish, there’s that fear: What if I get it wrong?
In those moments, grief stops being just a feeling. It settles in your chest, a tightness that lingers, even after the tears have faded. The world keeps spinning, but time seems to slow down right there in the aisles of H Mart—where what’s familiar and what’s foreign seem to collide. The longing for connection is as real as the smell of kimchi, and finding comfort turns into a journey through memory, culture, and all the complicated love between a mother and her child.
Most people don’t realize just how much of who we are is built on those small, everyday rituals with family. And for those who grow up straddling two worlds, those rituals are the only bridge to a heritage that’s both distant and deeply important. Losing a parent makes that bridge feel almost impossibly fragile. But holding onto those traditions—no matter how shaky it feels—is really just another way of holding onto yourself.
